headline: Rates Hold Near October Lows as Oil Prices Tumble
tileReason: The daily 30-year average edged down to 7.27% Friday as a tech-stock selloff sent money into bonds, and this morning oil is sliding on hopes for U.S.-Iran diplomacy.
takeaway: Mortgage rates are holding near their lowest levels in about six weeks. The daily 30-year average slipped 0.02% to 7.27% on Friday, and Freddie Mac's weekly survey (next update Thursday) sits at 7.24%. Friday's small dip came from another rough day for big tech stocks: after weak results from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel, the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 fell about 3.5%, and investors moved money into the safety of bonds. That helped the 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, finish October down roughly 0.36% to 0.40%, its best month for bond prices since 2024. Friday's official Treasury close was 4.94%. Two Federal Reserve officials, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan and St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem, said more rate hikes will be needed, which kept a December hike as the most likely outcome (futures put the odds at roughly 68% to 76%, depending on the source). This morning the big story is oil: crude is down about 4% after reports that President Trump wants to give talks with Iran more time, with Brent near $108 a barrel and U.S. crude just under $100, down from about $118 and $104 at Friday's close. Lower oil eases inflation worries. Working the other way, the October ISM factory survey came in stronger than expected at 55.5 (a reading above 50 means manufacturing is growing), though its measure of prices paid cooled. The 10-year yield is about 4.90%–4.92% this morning, slightly below Friday's close, which points to steady to slightly better lender pricing today. Mortgage rates are still unusually far above Treasuries: the Optimal Blue conforming index sat 2.17% above the 10-year on Oct 29, versus a long-run average of about 1.76%. Big tests this week: Tuesday's midterm elections and Friday's October jobs report.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Dec 9
fedOdds.afterLabel: Oct 30–Nov 2, after Fed officials Logan and Musalem called for more hikes
fedOdds.source: CME FedWatch via Trading Economics (Oct 30 and Nov 2), 24/7 Wall St (Oct 31) and Ivan Labrie Monday Brief (Oct 30 settle)
fedOdds.note: Odds of a quarter-point hike at the Dec 9 meeting were about 85% right after the Oct 28 hold, then eased as Treasury yields fell: about 68% at Friday's settle (Labrie), 72% Friday and about 75% Monday (Trading Economics), and about 76% (24/7 Wall St). Sources differ by several points, but a hike is still seen as the most likely outcome.

drivers.title: Tech selloff sends money into bonds
drivers.text: Shares of Alphabet, Amazon and Intel fell sharply after disappointing results, and the Nasdaq 100 dropped about 3.5% Friday, its worst day since June. Worries about heavy, debt-funded AI spending, including reports that a major AI company's expected credit rating may fall short of investment grade, pushed investors toward the safety of Treasuries. More demand for bonds lowers their yields, and mortgage rates follow, which is why the daily 30-year average ticked down to 7.27%.

drivers.title: Oil tumbles on hopes for U.S.-Iran talks
drivers.text: Crude is down about 4% this morning, with Brent near $108 a barrel and U.S. crude just under $100, after reports that President Trump wants to give diplomacy with Iran more time before any new strikes. Cheaper oil means lower gas and shipping costs, which eases inflation worries and tends to pull rates down. No deal has been announced, and Iran says the Strait of Hormuz stays closed until sanctions are lifted, so this can reverse quickly.

drivers.title: Two Fed officials call for more hikes
drivers.text: Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said she sees the need for at least two more quarter-point hikes, and St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said further tightening is needed soon because borrowing conditions are still too easy. When Fed officials lean toward higher short-term rates, investors expect higher rates across the board, which limits how far mortgage rates can fall. Futures still see a December hike as likely, at roughly 68% to 76%.

drivers.title: Factory survey comes in stronger than expected
drivers.text: The October ISM manufacturing index rose to 55.5 from 54.5, above forecasts in the mid-54s (above 50 means factories are expanding). A stronger economy tends to keep inflation and rates higher. The good news inside the report: the measure of prices factories pay fell to 75.2 from 77.9, a sign cost pressures may be easing a little.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat 2.17% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Oct 29, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap means lenders have room to lower rates if bond markets calm down, which is a cushion for borrowers even if Treasury yields stay where they are.

outlook.basis: Still close to a coin flip, with a slight lean toward rates staying about where they are and a very slight tilt lower. In borrowers' favor: Treasury yields just had their best month since 2024, tech stocks are shaky, oil is sliding on diplomacy hopes, and mortgage rates are unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.17% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%). Working against them: a December Fed hike is still seen as more likely than not, two Fed officials are openly calling for more hikes, the factory survey was strong, and inflation is well above target. Oil can rebound quickly if talks stall. Big swing events: Tuesday's midterm elections, the Nov 6 jobs report, the Nov 10 CPI report, and any news from the Iran talks.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average is about 7.27%, near its lowest in six weeks and down from roughly 7.5% in early October. A December Fed hike is still seen as likely, and this week's election and Friday's jobs report could bring bigger swings than usual, so it's worth asking your lender how locking, a float-down option, or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates have eased a bit, which helps affordability at the margin, but buyers are still stretched above 7%. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates are holding near six-week lows around 7.27% as bonds rallied and oil fell; the election and Friday's jobs report are the next big tests.
